readings.title: Exterior of the church
readings.locator: The Symbolism of the Church, p.xxvi
readings.text: The Exterior. A Temple has sometimes a single dome, sometimes many domes. One dome serves as a symbol of the One Head of the Church, Jesus Christ. Three domes typify the three Persons of the Holy Trinity. Five are symbolical of our Lord Jesus Christ and the Four Evangelists. Each dome—and where there is no dome the apex of the Temple—is crowned by a Cross, the emblem of victory.

readings.title: Altar and Gospel book
readings.locator: The Symbolism of the Church, p.xxviii
readings.text: Behind the Altar a seven-branched candelabra is usually placed (seven being the customary sacred number); and, sometimes a large Cross, for carrying in processions. The Book of the Holy Gospels, being the Word of God, is laid upon the Altar, to denote that God himself is mystically present thereon; and the Cross stands on the Altar as upon the place where is celebrated the unbloody sacrifice offered up to God.

readings.title: Lights
readings.locator: The Symbolism of the Church, p.xxxii
readings.text: Lights are always used during divine service, even though it be performed in full sunlight. This is done not only for illumination, but also to show that the Lord, who dwells in light ineffable, illumines the world with spiritual radiance; to denote that the hearts of faithful believers are warmed by a flame of love toward God and his Saints; and, also, to show forth spiritual joy and the triumph of the Church.

readings.title: How does Hapgood explain the domes?

paragraphs.text: The source gives symbolic interpretations of different numbers of domes: one for Christ, three for the Trinity and five for Christ with the four Evangelists. It also identifies the cross above the building with victory. These are the interpretations supplied by this historical account, not a requirement that every Orthodox church have the same exterior.

readings.title: Why are the Gospel book and cross associated with the altar?

paragraphs.text: Hapgood connects the Gospel book with the Word of God and the altar with the Eucharistic offering. Her description also mentions a seven-branched lampstand and a processional cross. The excerpt explains the significance assigned to these furnishings in the edition.

readings.title: Why are lights used in worship?

paragraphs.text: The commentary gives more than a practical explanation of illumination. It relates the lights to God’s light, love for God and the saints, and the joy of the Church. The distinction helps explain their presence even when daylight is sufficient.
